innovate

/IN-uh-vayt/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Innovate means to introduce new methods, ideas, or ways of doing something, especially within an existing field or process.

Rather than accept the confusing shift changes, the head nurse decided to innovate, introducing a bedside handoff method that cut medication errors in half.

Example

Water bills were draining the vineyard's budget, so Elena chose to innovate: she introduced a scheduling method that watered each row only when its soil sensors reported real thirst. The vines stayed just as healthy while water use fell by a third.

Elena does not build a brand-new machine; she introduces a new method for doing something the vineyard already did, and improving how an existing process works is exactly what it means to innovate.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

modernize: To modernize is to bring something up to date with the methods and technology already current, closing the gap with the present. To innovate is to introduce genuinely new methods or ideas, which may put you ahead of the current standard rather than merely level with it.

pioneer: To pioneer is to be among the very first anywhere to open up a new method or field, and the word crowns whoever got there first. To innovate is to bring new methods or ideas into how something is done, whether or not you are first in the world.

transform: To transform something is to change it so markedly that it looks or works like a different thing; the word measures the size of the change. To innovate names the act of introducing new methods or ideas, whether the change they bring is sweeping or modest.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

stagnate: to stop developing or improving

imitate: to copy what already exists

Where it sits · how deeply the old ways are changed

tinker → innovate → revolutionize

tinker vs. innovate: To tinker is to make small trial-and-error adjustments, while to innovate is to introduce genuinely new methods or ideas into how something is done.

revolutionize vs. innovate: To innovate is to improve how something is done, but to revolutionize is to change a whole field so completely that the old ways disappear.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-: into (Latin; not 'not' here)

Root — nov: from Latin novus, new

Suffix — -ate: verb-forming ending

Put it together: Innovate is built from in-, 'into,' plus the Latin root novus, 'new,' plus the verb ending -ate. To innovate is literally 'to bring newness into' something that already exists, which is why the word points at fresh methods and approaches rather than brand-new objects.

Use the root in a new word: novice: As a novice beekeeper, Dario asked endless questions during his first honey harvest; novice comes from the same Latin root, novus, meaning 'new,' that powers innovate.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral, common in business and science

Innovate is usually used without an object, as in 'the company must innovate to survive,' and it is about improving methods, ideas, or processes within something that already exists. Innovate focuses on new methods or approaches, often within an existing system, while invent means to create something entirely new that didn't exist before.
